title: The Gift of the Open Mind
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood recalls his work on the California Learning Assessment System reading test in the early 1990s, built on Langer's envisionment-building and Rosenblatt's aesthetic reading. The design dropped forced-choice items for open-ended responses, discussion and writing, culminating in the Open Mind, a blank circle where students show what a character is thinking. He relays Sheridan Blau's correction that texts construct readers, and that the strongest readers tolerate incompleteness and revise as they go. He narrates what the test felt like for a student reading Jackson's The Lottery, then recounts how CLAS was criticized and defunded in 1994 despite West Covina High's gains. He closes by arguing the effort deserves revisiting as a model for authentic, professional, regionally networked assessment, including of oral work.
points: The Open Mind item replaced pick-the-best-option testing with a free response, assessing how readers behave in a textworld rather than whether they find a right answer.
Blau's insight that texts construct readers shifted the aim to nuance and insight over right and wrong.
Top performance depended on tolerating incompleteness, suspending closure and revising understanding.
CLAS was killed after only two administrations, with criticism aimed at implementation and public education failures rather than the design itself.
The author wants authentic assessment, including of oral work, reconsidered as a way to professionalize schools in regional networks.
quotes: In the end there would be no pick-the-best-option on the reading test. The best option is what the reader takes freely. It struck me as poetic justice that this classiest of CLAS test items, the Open Mind, should involve an empty round circle, a bubble. I wish I knew who came up with the idea first or if it was imported. It was probably Fran, looking for a white crow.

No,” he said, “texts construct readers. You’ve got it reversed. We want to see how readers behave in the textworld, what they do with this space. There is no right or wrong. There’s nuanced, smart, there’s insight.

Nobody knew what behaviors we might see at more advanced levels. The most important trait turned out to be a willingness to suspend closure on an idea or inference, to tolerate incompleteness, to revise understandings as processing unfolded, to sit comfortably in confusion and challenge and improve unfolding envisionments.

The phenomenon of the ‘second read’ came to light. How many pieces of great literature exist that are read just once? Why insist on passages that no one has ever read? Why not aim for complex passages that reward multiple readings?

Incredibly, this assessment system still in its infancy was rolled out in 1993 and again in 1994. It was roundly criticized for its failure to educate the public about its radical nature, for its failure to implement smoothly, and for its failure to produce individual student scores. It could barely walk on its own.

Throughout its short life CLAS got negative press. The CLAS unit itself was blamed for problems far beyond its reach and charge. We know that CLAS was put on the shelf in 1994. Defund is the term these days. Not enough ink has been spilt to document this tragic whole-of-government failure to sustain a modest reform, in my humble opinion.

California made a conscious choice when it adopted the Common Core to place responsibility for resourcing and implementing assessment with districts, weakening the synergy that arises through large-scale projects.
